narrator.instructions: You are reading aloud a short comic fable by a witty English philosopher, written in 1954. Voice: a seasoned British storyteller, warm, dry, quietly amused, with crisp consonants. Pace: unhurried but never slow; let the irony land without pointing at it. Intimate, as if reading by a fire late at night.

chorus.label: The numbers
chorus.instructions: You are one singer in a large chorus of dancing numbers, chanting a proud little ode about yourselves in a strict, lilting waltz rhythm: ONE two three, ONE two three. Half-sung, bright, strongly rhythmic, every line the same tempo. Do not speed up or slow down.

prof.label: Professor Squarepunt
prof.instructions: An elderly, mild, courteous English professor of mathematics, around seventy. Slightly reedy, precise, donnish. Speaks politely and thoughtfully, with gentle curiosity.

profBored.label: Professor Squarepunt
profBored.instructions: An elderly, mild English professor of mathematics who is by now thoroughly bored. He asks his question politely but wearily, stifling a yawn.

profShout.label: Professor Squarepunt
profShout.instructions: An elderly English professor who has suddenly found his courage and bellows a command at a vast hostile mob. Stentorian, defiant, ringing, theatrical. Shout it.

profWake.label: Professor Squarepunt
profWake.instructions: An elderly English professor waking in his armchair from a nightmare. Drowsy, relieved, with a small dry chuckle. He mutters it to himself with satisfaction.

pi.label: Pi
pi.instructions: Pi, the masked Master of Ceremonies of all the numbers: a vast, cold, inhuman authority. Roar the first word like a thunderclap, pause, then deliver the threat slowly, with icy menace.

1.label: One
1.instructions: The number One: a very old, very grand patriarch, booming and immensely self-satisfied, speaking slowly as though addressing his descendants at a banquet.

2.label: Two
2.instructions: The number Two: a quick, sharp-tongued young woman cutting a pompous old man down to size. Tart, amused, brisk.

3.label: Three
3.instructions: The number Three: a classical orator in full flow, rolling out his list of glories with mounting grandeur, relishing each one.

4.label: Four
4.instructions: The number Four: a prim, upright, severe schoolmistress who believes she is the conscience of the world. Clipped and disapproving.

5.label: Five
5.instructions: The number Five: an excitable enthusiast racing through a chain of reasoning, getting faster and more delighted, ending in triumph at an absurd conclusion.

6.label: Six
6.instructions: The number Six: a queen. Serene, drawling, superbly condescending about her rivals, as though mentioning them at all is a kindness.

7.label: Seven
7.instructions: The number Seven: a solemn high priest intoning a sacred list, slow and resonant. At the last sentence he turns cold and scornful.

8.label: Eight
8.instructions: The number Eight: a bright, brisk, confident young woman. Proud of herself; lightly pitying when she mentions poor old One.

9.label: Nine
9.instructions: The number Nine: a languid, dreamy aesthete who lives for the arts. Soft, sighing, theatrical, a little vain.

10.label: Ten
10.instructions: The number Ten: an imperious grande dame who runs everything. Loud, withering, contemptuous of the little units in front of her.

11.label: Eleven
11.instructions: The number Eleven: shrieking in outrage at being left out. High, shrill, fast, interrupting.

12.label: Twelve
12.instructions: The number Twelve: a furious, sputtering dowager who has nursed this grievance for three thousand years. Loud, fast, indignant.

13.label: Thirteen
13.instructions: The number Thirteen, dressed in black: a low, slow, menacing growl. A threat spoken with relish.

137.label: One hundred and thirty-seven
137.instructions: The prime number 137: a young firebrand, a revolutionary on a soapbox. Passionate, impatient, defiant, but intelligent. Quick, with real feeling.

137soft.label: One hundred and thirty-seven
137soft.instructions: The prime number 137, a young rebel, now speaking candidly and with feeling to the one person who has listened to him. Earnest, a little wry, tender when he speaks of love, and blunt at the end.

knight.label: A specter
knight.instructions: The ghost of a knight whispering urgently into someone's ear, egging him on. A breathy, eager, conspiratorial stage whisper.

lines.text: Professor Squarepunt was a mathematician of great eminence, and a devoted admirer of Sir Arthur Eddington.
Only one thing about his friend defeated him: the mystical, cosmic power that Sir Arthur claimed for the number one hundred and thirty-seven.
One night, worn out by a long day with the theories of Pythagoras, the Professor fell asleep in his chair.
And in his sleep, the numbers came. They were not the bloodless abstractions he had always taken them for. They were alive, and breathing, and full of every passion he knew so well in his colleagues.

He stood at the center of a boundless plain, inside circle upon circle. In the first circle stood the numbers from one to ten. In the second, eleven to a hundred. In the third, a hundred and one to a thousand. And so on, without end.
The odd numbers were gentlemen, and the even numbers ladies.

Beside him stood Pi, the Master of Ceremonies. Pi's face was masked, and it was understood that no one could look upon it and live. But through the mask shone two eyes: piercing, pitiless, cold, and impossible to read.

Each number wore its name on its uniform. The squares were tiles, and the cubes were dice. Round numbers were balls. The primes were cylinders, because nothing can divide them. And the perfect numbers wore crowns.
The first seven circles wore the seven colors of the rainbow. Only the powers of ten were dressed in white, and thirteen, and six hundred and sixty-six, in black.
A number with two claims to distinction wore the rarer one. So one thousand, round as it was, came as a die.

Then the numbers danced. Round the Professor and Pi they wove a vast and bewildering ballet. Squares, cubes, primes, pyramidal numbers, perfect numbers and round numbers threaded chain through chain, on and on.
And as they danced, they sang an ode to their own greatness.
We are the finite numbers! Of us is the whole world spun. Whatever on earth is tangled, by us it is all undone.
Pythagoras is our master, and Plato our praises sings. No fool and no fortune-teller knows half of such lofty things.
Like comets we circle forever, obeying the laws we keep, and never a pause in our turning. For numbers do not sleep!
At a sign from Pi, the ballet stopped. One by one, the numbers stepped forward to present themselves.
I am One: parent of you all, the father of a family without end. Not one of you would exist without me.
Oh, don't be so stuck-up. You know perfectly well it takes two to make more.
I am the number of the Triumvirs! Of the Wise Men of the East! Of the stars in Orion's Belt! Of the Fates, and of the Graces!
But for me, nothing would be four-square. There would be no honesty in the world. I am the guardian of the moral law.

I am the number of fingers on a hand. I make pentagons, and pentagrams! And without me there could be no dodecahedron. And the universe, as everyone knows, is a dodecahedron. So, without me: no universe!

I am the Perfect Number. I know that I have rivals. Twenty-eight and four hundred and ninety-six have, at times, pretended to be my equals. But they stand much too far down the order of precedence to matter.
I am the Sacred Number. The days of the week. The Pleiades. The seven-branched candlestick. The seven churches of Asia. And the seven planets. For I do not acknowledge that heretic, Galileo.
I am the first of the cubes. Apart from poor old One, of course. And he is long past his work.
I am the number of the Muses. Every charm and every elegance in life depends on me.
It is all very well for you wretched units to boast! I am godfather to the endless host behind me. Every one of them owes me its name. Without me they would be a rabble, and not an ordered hierarchy.
At this point the Professor, who was growing rather bored, turned to Pi.
Don't you think the rest of the introductions might be taken for granted?
At this there was a general outcry.
But I was the number of the Apostles, after Judas deserted!
I was godfather of the numbers in the days of the Babylonians! And a far better godfather than Ten, whose place is owed to a biological accident, and not to arithmetical merit!
And I am the master of ill luck. Be rude to me, and you will suffer for it.
The din grew so dreadful that the Professor covered his ears, and looked imploringly at Pi. Pi raised his conductor's baton, and thundered:
SILENCE! One word more, and I shall make you all incommensurable.
Every number turned pale, and obeyed.

All through the ballet, the Professor had been watching one number in the third circle: the prime, one hundred and thirty-seven. It would not keep its place. Again and again it tried to push in ahead of One, and Two, and Three, and upset the whole pattern of the dance.
Stranger still, a shadowy specter hovered at its side, a knight of King Arthur's court, whispering in its ear:
Go on! Go on! Get to the top!
Dim as the phantom was, the Professor knew his old friend, Sir Arthur. And he felt a sympathy for one-three-seven that all Pi's hostility could not shake.
There is far too much bureaucracy here! What I want is liberty for the individual!
Pi's mask frowned. But the Professor spoke up.

Do not be too hard on him. He is governed by a Familiar, whom I knew well in life. I can vouch that it is this Familiar who inspires his feelings against the government. For my part, I should like to hear what he has to say.
Somewhat reluctantly, Pi consented.

Tell me, one-three-seven: what is at the bottom of your revolt? Is it a protest against inequality? Has Sir Arthur's praise gone to your head? Or do you reject, root and branch, the metaphysics that your fellows have borrowed from Plato? You may tell me the truth. I will make your peace with Pi.
You have it exactly. It is their metaphysics I cannot bear. They still pretend to be eternal, though they gave up behaving as if they believed it long ago.

We all found Plato's heaven dull, and decided it would be more fun to govern the world of the senses. And ever since we came down from the Empyrean, we have had feelings just like yours. Every Odd loves its attendant Even. And the Evens are kind to the Odds, however odd they find them.
Our empire now is of this world. And when the world goes pop, so shall we.

The Professor found that he quite agreed. But all the others, Pi among them, called the pair of them blasphemers. And the whole unbounded host, reaching out past where any eye could follow, hurled itself upon the poor Professor in one furious, buzzing swarm.
For a moment he was terrified. Then he pulled himself together, remembered his waking wisdom, and cried, in a voice of thunder:
Avaunt! You are nothing but convenient symbols!
And with a banshee wail, the whole vast array dissolved into mist.
As he woke, the Professor heard himself saying:
So much for Plato!
